sources.entry: Futexes Are Tricky - Derives a correct user-space mutex from futex and shows the lost wakeups and extra kernel entries naive versions pay.

summary.title: Futexes Are Tricky
summary.one_liner: Learn how the Linux futex system call works and why naive user-space mutexes built on it suffer lost wakeups and unnecessary kernel entries, using a step-by-step mutex design.
keywords: how to build a mutex with futex
why does my futex mutex sleep too often
takeaways: A futex is a 4-byte integer in user memory; the kernel's futex_wait and futex_wake operate on it, and the kernel only gets involved when waiting or waking is needed.
FUTEX_WAIT checks the futex value atomically before sleeping and returns EWOULDBLOCK if it has changed, which is the key to avoiding lost wakeups.

A simple atomic-increment mutex has two problems: it makes a system call on every unlock even when uncontended, and a race between the atomic check and entering the wait queue can cause endless retry loops.
FUTEX_WAKE_OP, FUTEX_CMP_REQUEUE and the obsolete FUTEX_REQUEUE cover cases such as condition variables, where waking and requeuing need more than one futex.
summary.summary: The article introduces the Linux futex kernel interface (FUTEX_WAIT, FUTEX_WAKE, FUTEX_WAKE_OP, FUTEX_CMP_REQUEUE, and others), explaining the atomicity guarantees the kernel provides around the futex value and its wait queue. It then builds a simple event object and a first mutex from atomic increment and futex calls, and verifies its correctness with thread-interleaving diagrams. The text then identifies the flaws: unnecessary unlock system calls under no contention and a race that can cause repeated EWOULDBLOCK retries, the latter costing heavy cache-line transfers. The rest of the document, beyond this excerpt, is said to fix these problems in a second version.
